[Section: **Origin of transverse corner cracks**] Several mechanisms causing transverse corner cracks are proposed in literature. Brimacombe [] comprehensively reviewed the stresses and strains in continuous casting that can give rise to cracks in the solidifying shell. Mechanical properties are affected by several factors, i.e. temperature, chemistry, microstructure, and thermal history.
[Section: **Origin of transverse corner cracks**] One of the proposed mechanisms is that the cracks are formed in the mould during initial solidification of the steel shell []. In general, local process disturbances related to mould heat transfer and slag infiltration as well as the depth of the oscillation marks may result in the formation of weak spots and transverse corner cracks []. This could be attributed to the chemistry of the steel, where manganese-sulfides can be formed. Harada et al [] present a thorough analysis of the formation of transverse cracks in conventional cast slabs in relation with manganese and sulfur content. The conclusion is that the cracks occur due to micro segregation of MnS in the oscillation mark. The degree of segregation was strongly affected by the depth of the oscillation mark. The MnS has a low melting point, making the grain structure in the oscillation mark weaker. It was advised to use slow cooling of the slab, a higher frequency and smaller stroke of the mould oscillation and avoid a Mn/S below 80.
[Section: **Origin of transverse corner cracks**] In a continuous caster the steel is subjected to a combination of thermal and mechanical deformation. Mechanically induced stresses can be caused by mould friction, ferrostatic pressure, machine condition i.e. roll pressure and misalignment, bending and unbending, and bulging. Additionally, thermal stresses, like temperature gradients in the shell and shrinkage associated with cooling, may lead to mechanical deformation of the shell. Transverse corner cracks can also originate when the strand is subjected to mechanical deformation in the secondary cooling area in the temperature range of the ductility trough [], especially when the slab is in the bending or unbending area. The precipitation of carbonitrides in steels alloyed with Al, Nb, Ti, and V, influences the low ductility of steels in this temperature range. The carbides and nitrides precipitate at the grain boundaries, making the steel brittle and crack sensitive. As long as the corners of the slab remain outside the ductility trough, the occurrence of transverse corner cracks can be reduced. During this study, trials were performed with straight narrow face copper plates, but they did not show an improvement in corner crack performance.
[Section: **Origin of transverse corner cracks**] Adaptations in secondary cooling can be made. Modern casting machines are equipped with width-dependent secondary cooling []. When this is not installed, width dependent cooling can be achieved by changing the nozzles at the sides of the slab [, ]. This leads to hotter slab corners and thus a reduced occurrence of corner cracks. Isaev et al [] indicate a clear dependence of the occurrence of transverse corner cracks on the slab width. They relate this to the over cooling of the slab edges when the width is too small, so they proposed a careful width dependent cooling.
[Section: **Origin of transverse corner cracks**] It should be noted that the weak spots in the shell as formed in the mould could be made visible as cracks in the secondary cooling area since due the uneven solidification, thermal stresses may arise upon further cooling. This underlines the need for stable casting operations in the mould, especially at the meniscus.

The nozzle modification prevents transverse corner cracks through two interconnected thermal-mechanical mechanisms. Second, the modified cooling profile reduces thermal gradients between the slab center and corners, minimizing thermal stresses that could activate pre-existing weak spots originating from the mold (such as MnS segregation in deep oscillation marks). The more uniform temperature distribution also reduces bulging by strengthening the central shell, further decreasing mechanical stresses at the vulnerable corners. This dual approach addresses both secondary cooling-induced cracking and potential propagation of mold-origin defects.

Implement a secondary cooling strategy with strong cooling in the initial cooling section followed by weak cooling in the subsequent warming section. This approach addresses the root cause of transverse corner cracks by manipulating the deformation-induced ferrite formation mechanism. During bending, dislocations accumulate at prior austenite grain boundaries, creating carbon fast channels that promote intergranular ferrite nucleation. The strong cooling in the initial section increases the ferrite film thickness along these boundaries, which initially lowers plasticity but then increases it as the film thickens, reducing stress concentration. The weak cooling in the warming section controls the reheating temperature below the Ac1 point, preventing austenite reformation and promoting ferrite formation within the grains. This homogenizes stress between grain boundaries and grains, minimizing the risk of crack initiation at corners where stress is highest. By optimizing this cooling profile, the slab's sub-surface microstructure develops with uniform stress distribution and enhanced plasticity, effectively eliminating corner cracks while preserving surface integrity.

The longitudinal surface cracks form through a synergistic embrittlement mechanism during straightening. The steel's inherently limited hot ductility, evidenced by reduction of area values consistently below 60% across the high-temperature range and dropping below 30% at 800-900°C, creates a material with minimal tolerance for plastic deformation. When combined with AlN precipitation occurring precisely in the 764-832°C temperature range - which coincides with the straightening operation temperature - the precipitates nucleate preferentially at austenite grain boundaries and sub-boundaries. These AlN particles act as stress concentrators and crack initiation sites. During straightening, the slab experiences tensile stress perpendicular to the casting direction. The columnar grain structure, aligned parallel to the casting direction, provides natural weak paths along grain boundaries where cracks can propagate longitudinally. The AlN precipitation at these boundaries further weakens the interfacial strength, causing cracks to follow the columnar grain alignment rather than propagating transversely. This mechanism differs fundamentally from transverse corner cracks, which typically originate from uneven cooling and thermal stress concentration at the slab corners during initial solidification in the mold.
